Synchrony 🇺🇸 United StatesPass

Price: $67.96 · P/E 7.1x (23 Nov 2026 close)

The case: A consumer-credit lender (store and co-branded cards) that has earned more than 11% on common equity in every year of the last ten, averaging about 20%, with capital well above the minimums. The cash-flow value is about 1.57 times the market value and still above it after a 25% cut, so it meets the bar. It is cheap because its profits depend on the US consumer: charge-offs run above 5% of loans, earnings fell by about two-thirds from 2019 to 2020, and it depends on a few large retail partners and on fee rules. The case fails if a recession pushes losses well above the 2020 level for several years.

Key figures: Net earnings to common shareholders 2016–2025: $2,251m, $1,935m, $2,790m, $3,747m, $1,343m (2020), $4,179m, $2,974m, $2,196m, $3,427m, $3,469m. Return on year-end common equity (total equity less preferred) 15.9%, 13.6%, 19.0%, 26.1%, 11.2%, 32.3%, 24.5%, 16.7%, 22.3%, 22.3%: average 20.4%, lowest 11.2%. Net interest income grew from $11,320m (2014) to $18,466m (2025). Owner earnings (ten-year average net earnings to common) $2,831m ÷ 7.5% = about $37.7bn, against a market value of about $24.0bn ($73.64 on 23 Oct 2026 × 325.4m shares): 1.57×, and 1.18× after a 25% cut. Common equity Tier 1 ratio 12.9% at 30 September 2026 (13.2% at 30 June; minimum 4.5%); Tier 1 leverage 13.0% at 30 June. Net charge-offs 4.79% of loans in Q3 2026 (5.43% in H1); 30+ days past due 4.34%. Q3 2026 net earnings $892m, diluted EPS $2.68 (Q3 2025: $2.86); quarterly dividend raised to $0.34. FT P/E 7.52.

Cheap on the latest year, but not steady quality on the ten-year record.

MARCOPOLO 🇧🇷 BrazilPass

Price: R$3.60 · P/E 4.2x (23 Nov 2026 close)

The case: Marcopolo, Brazil’s main bus-body maker with plants abroad, earns a high return on capital and has little industrial debt. On the multi-year average of its operating profit, which includes the weak 2022 year, the price gives an earnings yield of about 15%, and about 11% after a 25% cut, so it clears the Magic Formula bar with some room. It is cheap because bus demand is cyclical (EBIT was about a fifth of today’s level in 2022), margins are falling this year on a weaker sales mix, a stronger real and higher raw-material costs, overseas revenue fell 16% in the second quarter, and Brazilian interest rates are high. The pass is not wide: it depends on treating the Banco Moneo financing debt as matched by its loans (counting it, the average yield falls to about 12.4%, just under the bar), and it fails if earnings settle near the 2022–2023 level. The third quarter (profit down 43%, and no recovery expected into early 2027) moves earnings towards the weaker end of the range, so the risk that the average overstates normal earnings has grown; the pass stands on the four-year average for now, with lower industrial debt helping.

Key figures: Company-reported EBITDA (pre-tax result before financial income and expense, plus depreciation): R$385.6m (2022), R$946.9m (2023), R$1,625.2m (2024) and R$1,506.1m (2025, after a R$133.3m non-recurring charge from the Canadian associate NFI); first half 2026 R$643.3m against R$660.3m, so about R$1,489m over the last twelve months. Less depreciation and amortisation of R$119.8m, R$146.4m, R$167.6m and R$156.5m, operating EBIT was about R$266m, R$801m, R$1,458m and R$1,350m: positive every year, and the latest year 1.6 times the earlier three-year average, so not a one-off spike. Four-year average about R$968m. Market value about R$5.92bn (1,240.6m shares, all valued at the POMO4 price of R$4.77, 23 Oct 2026 close; the voting POMO3 shares trade lower at R$4.37). Industrial net financial debt R$475.1m at 30 June 2026 (0.3× EBITDA) and minority interests R$63m; the Banco Moneo financing arm’s debt is BNDES/FINAME on-lending matched by customer receivables and is left out, as the company reports it. Enterprise value about R$6.46bn: earnings yield about 21% on 2025 EBIT, about 15.0% on the four-year average, and 11.2% after a 25% cut in that average. Counting all consolidated net financial debt (R$3,404m borrowings less R$1,588m cash) instead, enterprise value is about R$7.80bn and the average yield about 12.4%. Return on invested capital 23.0% (company, last twelve months to June 2026). Q2 2026: revenue +3.0%, EBITDA −15.0% (margin 14.3% against 17.3%), net profit R$271.2m (−15.5%). Diluted EPS R$0.996 (2025); FT P/E 4.89. Q3 2026 (results, 3 Nov 2026): revenue R$2,293m (−8.5%), EBITDA R$274.1m (−34.7%; margin 12.0% against 16.8%, including R$19.9m of restructuring costs), net profit R$186.5m (−43.4%), production 3,085 units (−25.2%). That puts EBITDA for the twelve months to September at about R$1,343m. Industrial net debt R$341.1m at 30 September (R$475.1m in June); consolidated net debt including Banco Moneo R$1,799m. The company does not expect a consistent recovery in sales in late 2026 or early 2027.

INPEX CORP. 🇯🇵 JapanPass

Price: ¥3,254.00 · P/E 7.6x (24 Nov 2026 close)

The case: INPEX, Japan’s largest oil and gas producer (anchored by the Ichthys LNG project in Australia), is cheap on Greenblatt’s measure: even counting decommissioning obligations as debt, operating profit has been ¥1.06–1.25tn a year for four years and guidance for 2026 is similar, giving a pre-tax earnings yield of about 17%, and about 13% after a 25% cut. Debt is low. It passes the formula, but with two big caveats. First, the Magic Formula is pre-tax and INPEX pays more than half its pre-tax profit in tax, so the after-tax earnings yield is nearer 10%. Second, the earnings follow the oil and gas price: the four years read were years of firm energy prices, and the case fails if oil falls well below the US$60–70 range for long. It is cheap because the market treats upstream oil profits as cyclical, and because of the energy transition and Middle East risk.

Key figures: Operating profit ¥1,246bn (2022), ¥1,096bn (2023), ¥1,167bn (2024) and ¥1,063bn (2025) (Yahoo annuals); four-year average about ¥1,143bn. H1 2026 (results, 7 Aug 2026): revenue ¥1,000.5bn (−4.6%), operating profit ¥618.7bn (+0.3%), profit before tax ¥644.3bn, income tax ¥359.8bn (about 56% of pre-tax profit), profit attributable ¥263.1bn (+17.7%). FY2026 guidance raised to operating profit ¥1,223bn and net profit ¥510bn on Brent averaging US$81.4 (H2 US$75, Q4 US$70); the earlier low case (Brent US$70 for the year, H2 US$61) was ¥1,086bn. At 30 June 2026: bonds and borrowings ¥1,318bn, other financial liabilities (including leases) ¥148bn, asset retirement obligations ¥498bn, non-controlling interests ¥248bn, cash ¥216bn (another ¥744bn of current other financial assets not counted). Market value about ¥4.71tn at ¥4,049 (26 Oct 2026 close × 1,162.2m shares outside treasury at 30 June; buybacks since then cut the count by about 1%). Enterprise value about ¥6.70tn counting debt, leases, asset retirement obligations and minorities: normalised earnings yield about 17.1%, or 12.8% after a 25% cut; about 16% on the low-case 2026 guidance. Net debt about 0.7–0.8× EBITDA. FT P/E 10.43.

Natwest Group Plc 🇬🇧 LondonPass

Price: 591.00p · P/E 7.8x (23 Nov 2026 close)

The case: Lynch’s test is a growing company bought for less than its growth rate. NatWest has raised earnings per share every year since 2021, and even measured from pre-pandemic 2019 the growth rate is about twice the P/E; the 2026 nine-month profit is up again, with CET1 capital of 13.5% and low loan losses. It is cheap because UK bank earnings have been lifted by higher interest rates and buybacks, and the market doubts that growth lasts as rates fall; the 2020 loss shows how cyclical a bank is. The pass survives growth a quarter lower (PEG about 0.67), but if growth fell to Lynch’s 8% floor the PEG would be about 1, so this is a fair price for a cyclical grower, not a wide margin.

Key figures: Basic EPS 26.0p (2019, as RBS Group, before the 2022 share consolidation), a loss in 2020 (attributable loss £753m), then 25.4p (2021, 20-F), and diluted EPS 33.6p (2022), 47.7p, 53.1p and 67.4p (2025) on Yahoo’s annual figures: up every year from 2021 to 2025. Attributable profit £3,133m (2019), £2,950m (2021) and about £5.5bn (2025); fewer shares after buybacks account for part of the per-share growth. From 2019 to 2025 EPS grew about 16–17% a year (about 25% a year from 2021). Nine months to September 2026: attributable profit £4.6bn (£4.1bn a year earlier), Q3 EPS 19.3p, return on tangible equity 20.2%. CET1 ratio 13.5% at 30 September 2026 (target around 13%), liquidity coverage 137%, loan impairments 21bp of loans. FT P/E 7.99 at 597.2p (12 Nov 2026 close). PEG about 0.5 on 2019–2025 growth, about 0.67 with that growth cut by a quarter. Bank: debt test not applied; capital read instead.

It is cheap because of exposure to emerging-market currencies and politics (Haiti, Kenya, Nigeria, hyperinflation in some markets), fines such as the French Competition Authority’s Corsica decision, heavy solar spending, and the dilution in the governance change.

Key figures: Dividend per share €2.07 paid in June 2026 for 2025 (+2%), the company’s 30th consecutive yearly increase; calendar-year sums on the Yahoo dividend record rise every year from €0.35 (2005) to €2.03 (2025) and €2.07 (2026), plus a €0.75 exceptional interim in November 2024 from the Rubis Terminal sale. Yield about 5.8% (€2.07 / €35.48, 21 Oct 2026 close) against 2.8% for the MSCI index used for continental Europe. 2025: EBITDA €741m, net income Group share €309m, diluted EPS €2.98 (€3.30 in 2024 including the terminal gain; €2.50 excluding it). Cash flow from operations €734.8m, less capital spending of €375m (energy distribution €185m, renewable electricity €190m) and lease repayments of €48.4m, leaves free cash flow of about €311m against dividends paid of €220.7m plus €12.9m to minorities (1.33× cover). After a 25% fall in free cash flow, cover is about 1.0× on the €233.6m paid in 2025 and about 1.03× on the new €2.07 rate (about €214m on 103.2m shares, plus minorities); excluding the growth capex in renewables, which is partly funded by non-recourse project debt, cover is about 2.1×. Net financial debt €1,166m at December 2025 (1.7× EBITDA; corporate debt excluding non-recourse 0.9×), €1,466m at June 2026 (2.0×; corporate 1.3×) after the dividend; lease liabilities about €281m on top. H1 2026: EBITDA €434m (+18%), net income Group share €191m (+17%); adjusted operating cash flow €223m (−19%) on higher oil prices and working capital; FY2026 EBITDA guidance raised to €775–825m. On 19 October 2026 Rubis proposed converting into a société anonyme, with 12,719,328 new shares (about 12.3% of the capital) issued to the general partners, subject to the AMF and a shareholders’ meeting expected on 9 December 2026: at €2.07 on about 116.1m shares the dividend would cost about €240m plus minorities, and cover after a 25% fall in free cash flow would be about 0.9×. FT P/E 10.88.

Fail. Vistry passed again at 229.8p (19 October close), by about 1%. The shares then rose 5.7% to 243.0p on 20 October 2026, on heavy volume, the day it announced planning consent for the next phase of the Cambridge Road Estate scheme in Kingston. At that price the market value is about 0.70 times current assets less all liabilities, above Graham’s two-thirds entry line by about 21p a share (253.4p on 23 October), so it fails the formula. A fall back below about 232.6p would restore the pass.
